newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Bank of Israel vows no change in forex regime.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Israel vows no change in forex regime.

text.p: The Bank of Israel said on Sunday it was committed to the existing foreign exchange regime and would continue to defend the exchange rate.
The bank's statement came in response to Treasury director-general David Brodet's sharp criticism of monetary policy earlier on Sunday.
"The Bank of Israel will continue to absorb all excess liquidity in the economy with the tools that are available to it," the bank said.
"The Bank of Israel is committed to the exchange rate regime and within that framework - as well as its commitment to the government's inflation target - it will continue to defend the band."

The shekel is allowed to fluctuate in a trading band of seven percent above or below a sloping mid-point designed to devalue the Israeli currency at a rate of six percent a year against the basket of key currencies.

In the last two weeks the basket rate has been trading at the bottom of the band, forcing the central bank to intervene heavily in the local currency market. Brodet estimated the central bank injected as much as 3.5 billion shekels into the economy in January to defend the basket rate.

Bank officials have been denying persistent newspaper reports that the bank wants to widen the band. But the bank's statement did not address other reports that it wanted to increase reserve requirements or other measures.

Brodet blamed the bank's restrictive monetary policy of the last two years for Israel's slowing economic growth and the current problems with the exchange rate. But the central bank laid the blame on the Treasury.
"The problem of balance in Israeli economic policy is a result of the loss of fiscal control that began in 1995 and worsened in 1996," the Bank of Israel said.
Last year, the budget deficit reached 4.7 percent of gross domestic product, compared with a targeted level of 2.5 percent.

"This deviation in the target took place despite the warnings of the Bank of Israel and other economic bodies regarding its implications for the shekel and the balance-of-payments deficit," the central bank said.
